hints: Think about how an aromatic amine can be converted into a very good leaving group, recall what happens when $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ is treated with nitrous acid at low temperature.
Consider what happens when that diazonium intermediate is heated in aqueous solution, what nucleophile replaces nitrogen gas.
walkthrough:
Make the diazonium salt first**
You cannot turn $\text{-NH}_2$ directly into $\text{-OH}$. The trick is to turn it into $\text{-N}_2^+$ which leaves as $\text{N}_2$ gas very easily. Cool $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ to $0$ to $5\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ and add $\text{NaNO}_2$ plus $\text{HCl}$. In situ this makes $\text{HNO}_2$, nitrous acid, which diazotises the amine to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$.

Hydrolyse by warming in water**
Now warm that diazonium solution with water, above about $10\,^{\circ}\text{C}$. Water acts as the nucleophile, $\text{N}_2$ bubbles off, and you get phenol: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{N}_2 + \text{H}^+$$ Cold for step 1 to keep the diazonium ion stable, warm aqueous for step 2 to hydrolyse it.

Final answer: $\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{HCl}$ (forms $\text{HNO}_2$) at $0$ to $5\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ to form diazonium salt, then warm with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ at $T \geqslant 10\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ to give $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{N}_2 + \text{HCl}$.

hints: Recall that the $\text{-OH}$ group strongly activates the benzene ring, so phenol undergoes electrophilic substitution with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ at room temperature without concentrated acid or heating.
Think about which ring positions are activated by $\text{-OH}$, the $\text{-NO}_2$ electrophile can enter ortho or para to give isomers of formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_3$.
walkthrough:
See why conditions are so mild**
Benzene itself needs concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ plus concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and $50\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ for nitration. Phenol reacts with just dilute aqueous $\text{HNO}_3$ at room temperature. That tells you the $\text{-OH}$ lone pair is donated into the ring, making the ring much more electron rich and attractive to electrophiles.

Place the nitro group ortho and para**
The $\text{-OH}$ group is 2,4-directing. So mono-nitration gives two isomers with the same molecular formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_3$: 2-nitrophenol with $\text{OH}$ and $\text{NO}_2$ on adjacent carbons, and 4-nitrophenol with $\text{OH}$ and $\text{NO}_2$ opposite each other. Both keep the $\text{OH}$ intact, only ring H is replaced by $\text{NO}_2$.

Final answer: Products are 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol.
Structure 1: benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ at position 1 and $\text{NO}_2$ at position 2 (ortho). Structure 2: benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ at position 1 and $\text{NO}_2$ at position 4 (para).

hints: Remember that excess aqueous bromine with highly activated phenol gives multiple substitution, not just mono-substitution as with benzene.
Visualise the $\text{-OH}$ at position 1 and count the two ortho positions plus the para position where bromine atoms will substitute.
walkthrough:
Use all three activated positions**
With excess $\text{Br}_2$(aq), phenol is so reactive that substitution happens three times without any catalyst. Draw phenol with $\text{OH}$ at the top as C1. Then replace the H atoms at C2 (ortho), C4 (para) and C6 (ortho) with Br atoms.

Name it systematically**
Number from the $\text{OH}$ as 1 to give the lowest locants to the bromines. That gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol. The equation is: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 3\text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_2\text{Br}_3\text{OH} + 3\text{HBr}$$

Final answer: Structure: benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ at position 1 and $\text{Br}$ at positions 2, 4 and 6.
Name: 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

hints: Think about the colour of aqueous bromine before reaction and the physical state of the tribromo organic product in water.
walkthrough:
Link colour change to solid formation**
Aqueous bromine is orange. As $\text{Br}_2$ is consumed in the substitution, that orange colour fades. At the same time the product, 2,4,6-tribromophenol, is insoluble in water, so you see it as a white solid precipitating out. Both observations together are the classic positive test for phenol.
Final answer: Orange bromine water is decolourised and a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol is formed.

hints: Think of phenol donating its $\text{OH}$ proton to a strong base such as $\text{NaOH}$ to form a salt plus water, similar to a carboxylic acid but weaker.
walkthrough:
Write phenol acting as a proton donor**
Phenol is acidic enough to be neutralised by $\text{NaOH}$, though not by weak bases like $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ under normal criteria. The $\text{O-H}$ proton is transferred to $\text{OH}^-$: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ The organic product is sodium phenoxide. Check balance: one Na, one phenol unit and water on each side.

hints: Compare the stability of the anions left after $\text{H}^+$ loss, the more stable the conjugate base, the stronger the parent acid.
Think about what happens to the lone pair on oxygen in phenol and in the phenoxide ion, and how the benzene ring interacts with it.
Think about how the ethyl group in ethanol pushes electron density toward oxygen compared with H in water, and how that affects the $\text{O-H}$ bond strength and anion stability.
walkthrough:
Fix the order from anion stability**
Acidity is about how easily $\text{H}^+$ leaves: $$\text{HA} \rightarrow \text{H}^+ + \text{A}^-$$ If $\text{A}^-$ is stable, equilibrium lies further right. The correct order is phenol most acidic, then water, then ethanol least acidic.

Explain why phenol is strongest**
In $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, one lone pair on oxygen overlaps with the pi system of the ring. This delocalisation pulls electron density away from O, weakening the $\text{O-H}$ bond. More importantly, after deprotonation the negative charge on $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$ is delocalised into the ring, spreading and stabilising it. So phenol donates $\text{H}^+$ much more readily than water.

Explain why ethanol is weakest**
In $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, the ethyl group is electron donating by the positive inductive effect. It pushes electron density onto the oxygen, which strengthens the $\text{O-H}$ bond and intensifies the negative charge on $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-$, destabilising the anion. Water has no such donating group, so $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ loses $\text{H}^+$ more easily than ethanol but less easily than phenol.

Final answer: phenol > water > ethanol (most to least acidic).
In phenol, the lone pair on O is delocalised into the benzene ring, weakening the $\text{O-H}$ bond and stabilising the phenoxide anion, so $\text{H}^+$ is lost more easily.
In ethanol, the ethyl group has a positive inductive (electron donating) effect which strengthens the $\text{O-H}$ bond and destabilises the ethoxide anion, so $\text{H}^+$ is lost less easily than from water.
